In nearshore Hawaiian waters, the Hawaiian flagtail (Kuhlia sandvicensis) completes its early life stages with a remarkably small initial mass. Eggs hatch into yolk-sac larvae that weigh approximately 0.0045 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0045 grams] upon emergence, a value consistent with the modest egg diameters typical of many tropical perciform fishes. The liberated prolarvae remain entirely lecithotrophic during the first few days, absorbing endogenous yolk supplies before the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding commences. This larval phase, spent drifting as ichthyoplankton within the pelagic environment, is critical for survival, as feeding success at the time of yolk-sac resorption directly influences subsequent growth trajectories. Field surveys conducted across the main Hawaiian Islands indicate that these free-swimming exotrophic larvae experience high mortality rates, a common pattern among broadcast-spawning reef fishes that offsets the prodigious numbers of gametes released during each spawning event. The pelagic larval duration is relatively short compared to some congeneric species, allowing early recruits to settle onto shallow reef habitats while still quite small, where they begin the transition to a benthic, juvenile existence marked by rapid somatic development.

Sexual maturation in Hawaiian flagtail occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to many other reef-associated fishes. Based on otolith-derived growth data from populations around Oahu, puberty is attained at a total length of 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters], roughly corresponding to three years of age. This length at maturity translates into a wet weight at puberty of approximately 146.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 146.6 grams], according to length-weight regression models developed for this species which exhibit a slightly positive allometric relationship. The onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis are tightly linked to seasonal environmental cues, particularly fluctuations in water temperature and photoperiod. Reproductively viable adults typically undergo vitellogenesis and spermiation in synchrony with the summer months, ensuring that subsequent pelagic larval stages encounter favorable thermal conditions and adequate planktonic prey resources. This reproductive timing aligns well with patterns observed in other members of the family Kuhliidae, though Hawaiian flagtail appears to mature at a slightly larger size than its congener *Kuhlia mugil* from the South Pacific.

Adult Hawaiian flagtail can attain a substantial size for a species of this genus, with the maximum recorded total length reaching 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters]. This ultimate total length corresponds to an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 312 grams [Wwi = approximately 312 grams] for fully grown individuals, as derived from length-weight relationships parameterized from extensive sampling across Hawaiian archipelagic waters. Such a body size places K. sandvicensis among the larger members of its genus, though it remains considerably smaller than many other tropical reef fishes occupying similar trophic guilds. These reproductively active adults exhibit a generalized carnivorous diet, feeding primarily on crustaceans, small fishes, and benthic invertebrates, which supports the energetic demands of both somatic maintenance and gamete production. Field observations of marked individuals suggest that growth slows markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, with most additional length gain occurring during the first few years of life before approaching the asymptotic size. This growth pattern is typical of iteroparous teleosts that allocate a substantial fraction of ingested energy toward reproductive effort once the adult stage is reached.

Under the relatively stable thermal conditions characteristic of nearshore Hawaiian reef environments, typically around 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Hawaiian flagtail has been estimated from captive spawning trials and field-derived fecundity data. Females produce approximately 90 eggs daily [Ri = approximately 90 eggs daily] during peak spawning periods, a sustained output that reflects the high energetic investment this species makes in reproductive effort. This daily rate corresponds to a substantial annual fecundity, with individual females capable of releasing tens of thousands of pelagic eggs over the course of a single breeding season. The eggs are small, transparent, and possess a single oil globule, characteristics that facilitate buoyancy and dispersal within the planktonic realm. Spawning events are typically crepuscular, occurring around sunset in aggregations near reef channels or promontories, where gamete release and external fertilisation take place in the water column. This broadcast spawning strategy, combined with the high daily egg production rate, helps offset the considerable mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase and ensures adequate recruitment to maintain local population densities.

The maximum lifespan of Hawaiian flagtail in the wild has been documented through mark-recapture studies and otolith ageing techniques, with the oldest recorded individuals living for approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under natu at a temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]ral conditions. This longevity estimate was derived from fish maintained at ambient nearshore temperatures averaging 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], conditions that are typical of the species' core habitat throughout the Hawaiian Islands. Longevity reaches 96 months [am = 96 months] when conditions are favorable, placing this species among the longer-lived members of the genus Kuhlia at a temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. The natural mortality of senescent adults generally follows a period of gradual reproductive decline, with the oldest spawning individuals showing reduced fecundity and lower egg viability compared to prime-age adults. This pattern of reproductive senescence is consistent with the life-history strategy of an iteroparous, multiple-spawning teleost that experiences relatively low adult mortality rates in the absence of major predation pressure. Compared to other reef fishes of similar adult body mass, Hawaiian flagtail exhibits a moderately extended lifespan, falling within the range typical for medium-sized, non-specialist carnivores inhabiting tropical shallow-water environments. The combination of a 23-centimeter asymptotic length (23 centimeters) [Li = 23 centimeters] and an 8-year maximum lifespan places this species in a life-history continuum where delayed senescence is balanced against sustained reproductive output across multiple breeding seasons.
